Title: An agent-based simulation model of human–environment interactions in agricultural systems
Geographical_Context: Platform applications demonstrated across Chile, Germany, Ghana, Thailand, Uganda, and Vietnam
Agricultural_Domain: Crop and farm management; Agricultural technology adoption; Land and water management; Human–environment interactions
Study_Objective: Describe the Mathematical Programming-based Multi-Agent Systems (MP-MAS) software and demonstrate how it represents heterogeneous farm-household decision-making, agent interactions, markets, technology diffusion, and coupled agro-ecological dynamics.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Support ex-ante assessment of agricultural technologies, market dynamics, environmental change, and policy interventions while representing heterogeneous farm households and the natural resources they manage.
Agent_Types: Farm-household agents; simplified landowner/water-user-association actors; environmental/spatial entities
Agent_Roles: Farm-household agents make investment, production and consumption decisions; transact land and water rights; adopt technologies through social diffusion; optional environmental modules update water, soil, crop and livestock states.
Decision_Mechanism: Constrained mathematical programming for investment/production/consumption; adaptive expectations; local land/water auctions; threshold/frequency-dependent technology diffusion
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Farm households independently optimise expected farm/non-farm income subject to household consumption needs and resource constraints, update expectations from experience, and interact through local markets and innovation networks.
Input_Information: Land, labour, water, cash and livestock endowments; crop yields and prices; market inputs/outputs; technology characteristics; water rights; spatial plots; soil and hydrological state; household demographics
MAS_Platform_Technology: MP-MAS in C++; Excel input preparation; IBM OSL/COIN optimisation; optional TSPC, FAO CropWat, WASIM-ETH, LUCIA and EXPERT-N coupling through TDT
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: ODD/design concepts and software description, pp.3–17; agent objectives/adaptation and interactions, pp.12–14; environmental coupling, pp.21–25
Coordination_Mechanism: Local land and water markets/auctions; frequency-dependent technology diffusion; shared environmental-resource feedback
Communication_Mechanism: Market/bid-based exchange of land/water rights; innovation information diffusion through agent networks; environment-mediated feedback through coupled spatial/biophysical modules
Information_Shared: Technology-adoption information; market bids/shadow prices; land/water availability and rights; local resource/environment states
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Land; Irrigation water; Farm labour/cash; Agricultural technologies; Crop/livestock production resources
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Allocate scarce farm resources to income-maximising activities while representing market exchange, technology adoption, and environmental feedback under changing policy/climate/market conditions.
Conflict_Resolution: Land and water exchange is resolved through local auction mechanisms based on agents’ shadow prices/bids; other conflicts are represented through resource constraints and environmental feedback rather than collective bargaining.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Farm households compete for locally tradable land and water and for constrained household resources.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Water supply/rights; crop water requirements; irrigation technology; spatial water-flow conditions; expected yields/prices; farm resource constraints
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Agent–agent interaction, pp.13–14; water/land-market and environmental-coupling modules, pp.20–25
Agricultural_Outcomes: Farm income; technology adoption; crop/livestock production and land-use responses can be simulated across empirical applications.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Model supports assessment of water-saving technologies, land/water reallocation and resource-use adaptation; no single corpus-wide efficiency effect is reported.
Environmental_Outcomes: Soil, hydrological and other agro-ecological consequences of farm decisions are represented through optional/coupled environmental modules.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Water-saving technologies; alternative land/water allocation; policy interventions; coupled soil/hydrology feedback used for ex-ante impact assessment
Quantitative_Results: Illustrative northern-Thailand application reports simulated greenhouse adoption among farmers without land titles reaching nearly 77% by 2020 under credit without collateral versus about 36% under current conditions.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Farm income/technology adoption and resource use vs environmental externalities; individual farm optimisation vs collective resource outcomes
RQ3_Evidence_Locator: Empirical application examples and validation, pp.26–31; conclusions, pp.42–43
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Model validation; Comparative evaluation
Evaluation_Environment: MP-MAS applications across six empirical agricultural settings with alternative environmental modules and policy/technology scenarios.
Data_Source: Farm-household surveys; spatial/GIS and market data; crop/soil/water parameters; application-specific empirical datasets; default test dataset distributed with the software
Experimental_Scenarios: Multiple empirical applications addressing technology diffusion, land/water use, policy interventions and environmental change; alternative model features and coupled biophysical modules are compared.
Baselines_Comparators: Observed data for validation where available; current-condition/baseline scenarios; comparison with eight other human–environment simulators
Evaluation_Metrics: Observed-vs-simulated farm/land-use outcomes; technology-adoption trajectories; model construct/result validation; qualitative feature comparison among simulators
Evaluation_Results: The paper reports construct and result validation across applications and demonstrates that MP-MAS reproduces heterogeneous farm responses while integrating economic and environmental processes; application-specific examples illustrate technology diffusion and resource-use effects.
Evaluation_Scale: Six study-country applications; farm-household and plot level; spatial landscapes with optional water/soil/crop/livestock modules
Limitation_Categories: Scalability; Real-world validation; Other — limited collective decision-making; Other — limited actor diversity
Reported_Limitations: MP-MAS focuses primarily on farmer decision-making; non-farmer actors are simplified, agents cannot yet coordinate endogenous collective investments/actions, and some land-use behaviours such as encroachment are restricted by predefined ownership.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Extend group decision-making/user-association behaviour, collective investment/marketing, broader actor types and endogenous collective action.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Model validation, pp.29–31; software comparison and limitations, pp.35–42; conclusion, pp.42–43
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (B01). Platform/software overview rather than one single empirical experiment. Study-family reconciliation deferred to Step 5.

Title: 'Smart' policies to reduce pesticide use and avoid income trade-offs: An agent-based model applied to Thai agriculture
Authors: Christian Grovermann; Pepijn Schreinemachers; Suthathip Riwthong; Thomas Berger
Geographical_Context: Mae Sa watershed, northern Thailand; IPM reference data from Doi Angkhang, northern Thailand
Agricultural_Domain: Horticulture; Pesticide/IPM management; Agricultural policy; Farm economics
Study_Objective: Develop and validate an MP-MAS bio-economic agent-based model to ex-ante assess pesticide-reduction strategies and identify policy combinations that reduce pesticide use without harming farm household income.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Simulate heterogeneous farm responses to pesticide taxes, integrated pest management (IPM), price premiums, compensation and biopesticide subsidies, including innovation diffusion through farmer networks.
Agent_Roles: Farm agents choose crops, pesticide/input use, investments and IPM adoption subject to household resources; adoption spreads through innovation-network thresholds and observed population uptake.
Decision_Mechanism: Mathematical-programming income optimisation; adaptive expectations; pesticide production/damage-control functions; innovation-segment threshold rules for IPM diffusion
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Each farm household independently maximises income under land, labour, liquidity and other resource constraints, updates expectations over time, and adopts IPM when diffusion/network thresholds and profitability conditions are met.
Input_Information: Farm household survey data; land/labour/liquidity; crop rotations; pesticide prices/toxicity and production functions; IPM costs/yields/prices; market expectations; innovation-network/adopter thresholds
MAS_Platform_Technology: MP-MAS; econometrically estimated production/damage-control functions; Monte Carlo agent-population generation
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Methods Sections 3.1–3.6, pp.94–98; model implementation and agent-population description, pp.94–96
Coordination_Mechanism: Social/innovation-network diffusion of IPM adoption; no explicit shared-resource allocation or negotiation mechanism.
Communication_Mechanism: Indirect/social-network diffusion: farm agents observe population adoption and innovation information through network/adopter thresholds.
Information_Shared: IPM/innovation adoption information; expected prices/yields; technology characteristics
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Pesticide use; IPM adoption; farm land/labour/liquidity; crop production
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Reduce pesticide use/toxicity while maintaining farm income and feasible use of household resources.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Farm households face competing uses of land, labour and liquidity and heterogeneous incentives to adopt IPM; direct competition among agents is not modelled.
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Methods Sections 3.2–3.6, pp.95–98; IPM adoption/diffusion and resource constraints
Agricultural_Outcomes: Farm income; crop/land-use patterns; IPM adoption; pesticide use and toxicity
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Lower chemical pesticide use and substitution toward IPM/biopesticides while maintaining or increasing average income under selected policy packages.
Environmental_Outcomes: Reduced pesticide use and especially highly toxic pesticide use, implying lower environmental and human-health exposure.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Progressive toxicity-based pesticide tax; IPM diffusion/promotion; biopesticide subsidy; price premium or direct compensation
Quantitative_Results: With IPM + progressive tax + 80% biopesticide subsidy, authors report pesticide use in period 5 reduced by about 34%; Table 9 reports total pesticide use −29.0% and highly toxic pesticide use −34.3% in period 5, while average household income increased 8.7% versus baseline.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Pesticide/toxicity reduction vs farm income and policy cost; distributional differences in who gains from IPM adoption
RQ3_Evidence_Locator: Results Sections 4.1–4.2, pp.99–101; Table 9 and Figure 7; Conclusion, p.102
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Model validation; Comparative policy evaluation
Evaluation_Environment: MP-MAS representation of the Mae Sa horticultural economy with a synthetic population of farm households and empirically estimated pesticide/IPM response functions.
Data_Source: Survey of 295 Mae Sa farm households; supplementary IPM survey at Doi Angkhang; pesticide trader/shop/producer data; production and toxicity data
Experimental_Scenarios: Progressive pesticide-tax levels; IPM introduction; direct compensation; price premiums; 60%/80% biopesticide subsidies and combined policy packages.
Baselines_Comparators: Baseline without interventions; tax-only; IPM-only; alternative compensation/subsidy packages
Evaluation_Metrics: Land use; sales revenue; pesticide use; highly toxic pesticide use; farm income; tax revenues; policy costs; IPM area/adopter group; observed-vs-simulated goodness of fit
Evaluation_Results: Baseline validation against survey data showed close agreement for land use, sales revenue and pesticide use; combined smart-policy packages substantially reduced pesticide use while avoiding aggregate income losses.
Evaluation_Scale: 1,491 simulated farm-household agents generated from a 295-household survey; five simulation periods; watershed-scale horticultural system
Limitation_Categories: Uncertainty; Environmental modelling; Real-world validation; Other — simplified farmer behaviour
Reported_Limitations: Income maximisation is a simplifying behavioural assumption; risk behaviour and farmer learning could be represented better; pest pressure–pesticide–yield relationships omit biological mechanisms such as resistance and predator–prey dynamics.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Improve risk/learning representation and pest-pressure/yield-damage ecology; extend IPM evidence to additional crops and settings.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Model verification/validation Section 3.8, pp.98–99; Discussion, pp.101–102; supplementary-data/software statements
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (B02). Study-family reconciliation deferred to Step 5.

Title: Ex-ante assessment of soil conservation methods in the uplands of Vietnam: An agent-based modeling approach
Authors: Dang Viet Quang; Pepijn Schreinemachers; Thomas Berger
Agricultural_Domain: Crop and farm management; Soil conservation; Soil fertility/erosion; Technology adoption
Study_Objective: Use an integrated MP-MAS–soil model to assess long-term soil erosion and farm-income dynamics, adoption constraints for soil-conservation practices, and monetary incentives required to reduce erosion.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Simulate heterogeneous farm-household decisions, technology diffusion and soil-fertility feedback to evaluate soil-conservation practices and incentive policies ex ante.
Agent_Roles: Farm agents choose investments, crops and soil-conservation practices while satisfying household rice needs and maximising cash income; fields/soil modules update fertility, erosion and crop yields; adoption spreads through social-network diffusion.
Decision_Mechanism: Mathematical-programming farm optimisation; adaptive expectations; threshold/network-based technology diffusion; TSPC soil-fertility/yield feedback
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Each of 471 farm-household agents independently makes investment/production decisions under resource constraints and uncertain expected yields/prices, while technology adoption is conditioned by network diffusion and profitability.
Input_Information: Farm-household resources and survey data; land/field location; crop prices/yields; labour and cash; soil nutrients/fertility; erosion parameters; livestock/perennial assets; technology-adoption characteristics
MAS_Platform_Technology: MP-MAS coupled with Tropical Soil Productivity Calculator (TSPC); spatial grid; downloadable executable/input files and technical documentation
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Model description Sections 2.1–2.3, pp.110–114; agent decision-making, technology diffusion and TSPC coupling
Coordination_Mechanism: Social-network/technology-diffusion mechanism plus environment-mediated coupling between farm decisions and shared landscape/soil dynamics.
Communication_Mechanism: Innovation information diffuses through farm-agent social networks; agent–environment interaction occurs through spatial soil-fertility and crop-yield feedback.
Information_Shared: Technology-adoption information; prior adoption levels; expected yields/prices; field/soil state indirectly through environmental feedback
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Agricultural land; Soil fertility; Farm labour/cash; Soil-conservation technology adoption
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Maintain farm livelihoods and crop production while reducing soil erosion and identifying economically feasible conservation adoption.
Conflict_Resolution: No explicit bargaining; adoption and resource conflicts are resolved through household optimisation, incentive scenarios and diffusion constraints.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Farm household consumption/income needs compete with long-term soil-conservation objectives and short-term yield/labour costs.
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Design concepts and agent–agent/environment interaction, Sections 2.1.4 and 2.2.1–2.2.3, pp.111–114
Agricultural_Outcomes: Crop yields; household/farm income; adoption of vetiver, ruzi grass and leucaena conservation practices
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Conservation scenarios reduce soil/nutrient loss and preserve productive soil resources; adoption is strongly constrained by yield effects.
Environmental_Outcomes: Soil erosion; N/P/K nutrient loss; long-term soil fertility decline
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Soil-conservation strips/hedges; monetary incentives for adoption; technology diffusion and field-level soil feedback
Quantitative_Results: Baseline erosion averaged 29.97 t/ha/year for maize and 26.64 t/ha/year for cassava; average maize/cassava income fell 28.5% from 456 to 326 USD/ha over 25 years. Payments of roughly 12–16 USD per ton of soil saved were estimated to achieve about a 40±2% reduction in soil loss.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Short-term crop yield/income and labour requirements vs long-term soil conservation; public incentive cost vs erosion reduction
RQ3_Evidence_Locator: Results Sections 4.1–4.3, pp.114–117; Table 3 and Figure 7; Discussion/Conclusion, pp.117–118
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Model validation; Scenario/sensitivity analysis
Evaluation_Environment: Spatial MP-MAS/TSPC simulation of 471 farm households and their fields over a 25-year horizon.
Data_Source: 2007/2008 survey of 159 households; full 471-household commune population generated by Monte Carlo; field/soil experiments; secondary agronomic data
Experimental_Scenarios: Baseline plus three soil-conservation technologies; altered yield/labour assumptions; multiple monetary-incentive levels for adoption.
Baselines_Comparators: Observed data for model validation; baseline without conservation; alternative conservation technologies and incentive levels
Evaluation_Metrics: Observed-vs-simulated household/land-use outcomes; soil and nutrient loss; crop yield; farm income; adoption area; payment per ton of soil saved
Evaluation_Results: Model validation was satisfactory for key socioeconomic/biophysical variables; simulations reproduced observed-range erosion and showed that conservation adoption is highly sensitive to yield effects and economic incentives.
Evaluation_Scale: 471 farm-household agents; 159-household empirical survey; spatial commune landscape; 25 simulation periods/years
Limitation_Categories: Uncertainty; Environmental modelling; Real-world validation; Other — behavioural simplification; Other — transferability of conservation parameters
Reported_Limitations: Profit/income maximisation is a simplifying behavioural assumption. Local data on conservation-practice effects were unavailable, so effects on maize yield/erosion were transferred from Thai uplands; results are especially sensitive to assumed yield impacts.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Field-test the most promising conservation practices locally, improve locally calibrated conservation-effect parameters, and strengthen behavioural representation beyond simplified profit maximisation.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Model validation Section 3, pp.114–115; Discussion, pp.117–118; software/input availability, p.111
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (B03). Study-family reconciliation deferred to Step 5.

Title: An agent-based simulation of cooperation in the use of irrigation systems
Geographical_Context: Chinese irrigation villages, with calibration/field evidence from central China including the Third Dongfeng Canal, Dangyang, Hubei
Agricultural_Domain: Irrigation/water management; Water-user cooperation; Common-pool resource governance
Study_Objective: Develop an agent-based model of how farmer households form cooperation in irrigation management and evaluate how seed participants, government support, household characteristics and village network structure affect cooperation diffusion.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Explain and simulate emergence of collective irrigation management/Water User Association participation among autonomous farmer households.
Contribution_Type: Simulation model; Coordination/cooperation mechanism; Policy-evaluation framework
Agent_Types: Farmer-household/water-user agents; government entity; irrigation-resource entity; social-network/environment entity
Agent_Roles: Farmer agents decide whether to join irrigation cooperation based on affordability, propensity, personal characteristics and participating neighbours; government subsidises cooperation costs; the irrigation/social environment carries network and resource context.
Decision_Mechanism: Threshold/probabilistic participation rules combining willingness-to-pay, entrepreneurship/resource dependence/distance and neighbourhood effects; government-subsidy parameter
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Households autonomously decide whether to join cooperation; decisions are conditioned by their own characteristics, cooperation cost and the participation of network neighbours.
Input_Information: Household socio-economic characteristics; willingness/ability to pay; distance/resource dependence; social-network ties; neighbour participation; cooperation fee/cost; government subsidy ratio
MAS_Platform_Technology: NetLogo; ODD protocol model; public model on OpenABM
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: ODD model description: purpose/entities/process/design concepts, pp.7–12; NetLogo implementation, p.12
Coordination_Mechanism: Neighbourhood/social-network diffusion of cooperation; collective Water User Association formation; government cost subsidy
Communication_Mechanism: Neighbour-mediated social influence/observation within random or scale-free village networks; no formal message protocol.
Information_Shared: Whether neighbours have joined cooperation; local social-network participation state; cooperation cost/subsidy conditions
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Collective irrigation-system use and management; participation in Water User Association/cooperation
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Achieve viable collective management of irrigation infrastructure/resources by increasing participation and reducing individual coordination costs.
Conflict_Resolution: Collective-action failure is addressed by cooperation participation, neighbour effects and government subsidies that lower the individual cost of joining.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Individual household incentives/costs vs collective irrigation-system sustainability and group participation.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Cooperation fee; government subsidy; resource dependence; household distance; neighbour participation and network position
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Formation mechanism and process scheduling, pp.5–10; ODD design concepts, pp.10–12
Agricultural_Outcomes: No direct crop/yield outcome is simulated; outcome is farmer participation in cooperative irrigation management.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Collective irrigation governance is intended to improve sustainable management of the irrigation resource; direct water-saving quantities are not reported.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Collective Water User Association/cooperation and government support for shared irrigation management
Quantitative_Results: Across 38,400 parameter combinations run 100 times each (3.84 million simulations), a subsidy exceeding 50% of cooperation costs led to roughly 80% eventual participation; the initial seed-participant ratio had little effect.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Individual cooperation cost/affordability vs collective irrigation-system benefits; government subsidy dependence vs self-organised participation
RQ3_Evidence_Locator: Results, pp.12–17; Discussion, pp.17–21; Conclusions, p.21
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Parameter sweep; Regression analysis
Evaluation_Environment: NetLogo social-network model calibrated with field/survey evidence on Chinese irrigation villages and WUAs.
Data_Source: 2014–2015 field surveys across 180 villages/14 provinces (>500 questionnaires and >30 interviews/focus groups); detailed central-China WUA cases; literature-derived parameters
Experimental_Scenarios: Random vs scale-free networks; three seed-participant types; seed ratios; government subsidy ratios; cooperation-propensity/cost parameters; village sizes and network characteristics.
Baselines_Comparators: Alternative network structures, seed-participant types/ratios and subsidy levels; no single external algorithmic baseline
Evaluation_Metrics: Participation rate; speed of participation; regression coefficients/significance for subsidy, seed, network and household parameters
Evaluation_Results: Government subsidy robustly increased both reach and speed of cooperation diffusion, while seed-participant ratio/type had little effect; network and household factors also shaped diffusion.
Evaluation_Scale: 3.84 million simulation runs from 38,400 parameter combinations ×100 replications; field calibration from village/WUA survey data
Limitation_Categories: Real-world validation; Uncertainty; Other — stylised cooperation mechanism; Adoption/usability
Reported_Limitations: The model is stylised around cooperation diffusion and does not model broader operational irrigation outcomes; findings are calibrated to successful WUA cases and depend on assumed behavioural/network mechanisms and government support.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Test cooperation mechanisms in more diverse/less successful irrigation contexts and examine how government support can foster cooperation without creating long-term dependence.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: ODD initialization/inputs and public model, pp.12–13; Results/robust regressions, pp.12–17; Discussion/Conclusions, pp.17–21
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (B04). Study-family reconciliation deferred to Step 5.

Title: Water management for irrigation, crop yield and social attitudes: a socio-agricultural agent-based model to explore a collective action problem
Authors: Lucia Tamburino; Giuliano Di Baldassarre; Giulia Vico
Geographical_Context: Lower Mississippi River Basin, USA (model calibration context)
Agricultural_Domain: Irrigation/water management; Groundwater management; Crop production; Socio-hydrology
Study_Objective: Develop a socio-agricultural agent-based model to explore how farmer time orientation and irrigation-source choices create collective-action dynamics affecting crop yield, groundwater decline and farm economics under current and future climates.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Simulate community-level consequences of individual choices between groundwater wells and on-farm ponds and identify when sustainable water-use behaviour benefits individual farmers and the community.
Contribution_Type: Simulation model; Socio-hydrological framework; Policy/collective-action analysis
Agent_Types: Farmer agents; farm/crop entities; shared groundwater resource
Agent_Roles: Farmers choose irrigation infrastructure/source and may adapt their short-/long-view attitude from past yield/economic experience; farms generate crop yield/economic outcomes; the shared aquifer is depleted by aggregate groundwater withdrawals.
Decision_Mechanism: Behavioural short-/long-view decision rules; experience/memory-based attitude updating; water-balance and crop-yield equations
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Each farmer independently selects/maintains wells or on-farm ponds according to attitude and financial resources; agents do not directly communicate but jointly affect the common aquifer through withdrawals.
Input_Information: Farmer long-/short-view parameter and memory; capital; well/pond costs; soil water; rainfall and temperature; crop water need/yield response; groundwater depth; farm area
MAS_Platform_Technology: Custom socio-agricultural agent-based simulation coupled to soil-water, crop-yield, groundwater and farm-economy equations
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Methods Sections 2.1–2.3, pp.1817–1821; conceptual model and farmer attitude/infrastructure rules
Coordination_Mechanism: Environment-mediated implicit coordination/competition through shared groundwater depletion; no direct agent-to-agent communication or negotiation.
Communication_Mechanism: Environment-mediated/indirect only: farmers affect one another through the common groundwater table.
Information_Shared: No direct information sharing; the shared aquifer state aggregates community withdrawals, while individual farmers use own experience/memory.
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Groundwater; On-farm stored water; Irrigation-source choice; Cultivated land
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Maintain crop production and stable farm income while slowing shared groundwater depletion and avoiding tragedy-of-the-commons dynamics.
Conflict_Resolution: No explicit bargaining; collective conflict is resolved only through individual adoption of ponds/long-view behaviour and resulting shared-resource feedback.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: 121 farmers draw from the same declining aquifer; individual cultivated-area/profit incentives conflict with community groundwater sustainability.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Rainfall; crop water requirement; soil-water availability; groundwater depth/well access; pond capacity; farmer capital; attitude/memory; climate scenario
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Conceptual model and infrastructure/attitude decisions, Sections 2.1–2.3, pp.1817–1821; community resource feedback in Results Section 3.2
Agricultural_Outcomes: Crop yield; cultivated area; net economic gain; yield/income stability under different farmer-attitude and climate conditions
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: On-farm ponds reduce dependence on shared groundwater and slow aquifer depletion at the cost of cultivated area and capital investment.
Environmental_Outcomes: Groundwater-table decline and long-term aquifer depletion under alternative farmer-community compositions and climate scenarios
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Adoption of on-farm ponds; long-view farmer behaviour; potential incentives for pond construction
Quantitative_Results: Model simulations used 121 farmers (3.5 ha each), 100 replications per parameter combination over 30 years. Under the extreme climate scenario, long-view-oriented farming produced higher average net economic gains when the short-view-farmer ratio exceeded about 0.45; higher short-view ratios consistently accelerated groundwater decline.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Individual short-term yield/profit and cultivated area vs long-term groundwater preservation and income stability; pond investment/land loss vs collective aquifer benefits
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Scenario analysis; Sensitivity/behavioural comparison
Evaluation_Environment: Stylised socio-agricultural community calibrated to Lower Mississippi River Basin hydrologic/agricultural conditions.
Data_Source: Published/empirical Lower Mississippi parameter values and supplementary parameterisation; synthetic stochastic rainfall/climate series; model-generated farmer communities
Experimental_Scenarios: Current, intermediate and extreme climates; varying proportions of short-view farmers; different initial groundwater depths; fixed vs experience-adapting farmer attitudes.
Baselines_Comparators: Short-view vs long-view farmers; communities with different short-view ratios; current vs drier climate scenarios; fixed vs evolving attitudes
Evaluation_Metrics: Crop yield; groundwater depth; average and variability of net economic gain; farmer-attitude composition
Evaluation_Results: Short-view groundwater-dependent behaviour often maximised individual short-term returns but accelerated aquifer decline and destabilised community outcomes; long-view/pond behaviour improved collective sustainability and becomes individually advantageous under sufficiently severe climate stress.
Evaluation_Scale: 121 farmers, 3.5 ha each; 30-year simulations; 100 stochastic replications per parameter combination
Limitation_Categories: Environmental modelling; Uncertainty; Real-world validation; Other — stylised homogeneous farms/behaviour
Reported_Limitations: The model intentionally simplifies crop growth and hydrology, assumes farms identical in size/pedoclimatic conditions and focuses on one crop; groundwater recharge and pond hydrology are simplified, and farmer attitude/memory is stylised.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Empirically test farmer-attitude dynamics and policy incentives; extend to heterogeneous farms/crops and richer groundwater/pond hydrology.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Model parameterisation/simulations Section 2.3, pp.1820–1821; Results/Discussion Section 3, pp.1821–1827; Conclusions, pp.1827–1828
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (B05). Interaction is indirect through the shared aquifer rather than direct communication. Study-family reconciliation deferred to Step 5.

Title: An agent-based model of farmer decision-making and water quality impacts at the watershed scale under markets for carbon allowances and a second-generation biofuel crop
Authors: Tze Ling Ng; J. Wayland Eheart; Ximing Cai; John B. Braden
Geographical_Context: Salt Creek Watershed, Central Illinois, USA (semi-hypothetical farmer population)
Agricultural_Domain: Crop and farm management; Water quality; Bioenergy crop adoption; Best-management practices; Carbon markets
Study_Objective: Develop an agent-based farmer decision model coupled to a hydrologic-agronomic watershed model to examine how farmer behaviour, social interaction and markets for crops/carbon/miscanthus affect land-management decisions and stream nitrate loads.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Represent heterogeneous adaptive farmer decisions and innovation diffusion to evaluate watershed-scale agricultural and water-quality outcomes under market/policy scenarios.
Contribution_Type: Simulation model; Policy-evaluation framework; Coupled socio-hydrological/agronomic model
Agent_Roles: Farmers choose crops and BMPs, update price/cost/yield/weather expectations using Bayesian inference, share information with spatial neighbours, and decide whether to adopt unfamiliar activities such as miscanthus, carbon trading and conservation tillage.
Decision_Mechanism: Mean–variance utility optimisation; Bayesian updating of expectations/uncertainty; neighbour information exchange; risk-aversion and bold/cautious behavioural profiles
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Each farmer independently maximises expected utility over crop/BMP choices under risk and multi-year commitments, updates beliefs from personal and neighbour observations, and controls one watershed subbasin/farm.
Input_Information: Crop/fertiliser/carbon prices; production costs; crop yields; weather; risk aversion; discount rate/foresight; farm area/marginal land; neighbour observations; SWAT soil/hydrology/nutrient states
MAS_Platform_Technology: Custom agent-based farmer model coupled to SWAT hydrologic-agronomic watershed model; Bayesian inference and economic optimisation
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Sections 3.2–3.4, pp.4–10; farmer utility/Bayesian adaptation and multiple-farmer model
Coordination_Mechanism: Neighbour-to-neighbour information exchange and innovation diffusion; coupled watershed feedback from aggregate land-management decisions.
Communication_Mechanism: Direct/local neighbour information sharing: farmers exchange observed cost, yield and price information; unfamiliar-activity uncertainty falls as self/neighbours gain experience.
Information_Shared: Costs; yields; selected prices; experience with miscanthus, conservation tillage and carbon trading; observations used for Bayesian belief updates
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Crop/BMP choice; agricultural land; fertiliser/nitrogen management; adoption of miscanthus/conservation tillage/carbon trading
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Maximise farmer expected utility/returns while assessing emergent land-use adoption and watershed nitrate outcomes under changing crop and carbon markets.
Conflict_Resolution: No explicit negotiation; coordination emerges through information sharing, market signals and coupled environmental feedback.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Farmers face competing crop/BMP returns and risk; aggregate decisions create watershed water-quality externalities rather than direct resource competition.
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Section 3.4.2 Interactions Between Farmers, pp.9–10; coupled farmer–watershed feedback, Sections 3–4
Agricultural_Outcomes: Adoption of corn, soybeans and miscanthus; conservation tillage/grassland decisions; farm-level responses to crop/carbon prices and behavioural profiles
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Conservation tillage/miscanthus scenarios can reduce nitrogen losses while changing land allocation; explicit input-efficiency metric NR.
Environmental_Outcomes: Stream nitrate load at the watershed outlet under alternative market prices, farmer learning/interaction and BMP adoption.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Miscanthus adoption; conservation tillage; uncultivated grass; carbon allowance incentives; farmer information diffusion
Quantitative_Results: For miscanthus-price ratio 0.5 and zero carbon price, average annual nitrate load was 6.30×10^3 t N/yr with perfect-foresight farmers, 7.86×10^3 with adaptive farmers, and 10.12×10^3 with stationary farmers; interacting/bolder populations adopted unfamiliar practices faster.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Farm profitability/market response and risk vs nitrate/water-quality improvement; rapid innovation adoption vs behavioural uncertainty
RQ3_Evidence_Locator: Results Sections 4.1–4.2, pp.10–14; Table 2 and Figures 5–7
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Sensitivity analysis; Comparative behavioural evaluation
Evaluation_Environment: Agent-based model of 50 hypothetical heterogeneous farmers coupled one-to-one with agricultural subbasins of a calibrated SWAT model for Salt Creek Watershed.
Data_Source: Historical watershed hydrology/water-quality and agricultural data for SWAT calibration; crop/price/cost/yield scenarios; semi-hypothetical farmer attributes and behavioural assumptions
Experimental_Scenarios: Sensitivity analysis over 18 input-variable sets; different bold/cautious population mixes; interacting vs non-interacting farmers; adaptive vs stationary vs perfect-foresight behaviour; multiple carbon and miscanthus prices.
Baselines_Comparators: Perfect-foresight and stationary farmers; interacting vs non-interacting populations; alternative bold/cautious mixes; multiple price scenarios
Evaluation_Metrics: Crop/BMP adoption fractions; conservation/carbon participation; stream nitrate load; sensitivity of decisions to prices, costs, yields and behavioural parameters
Evaluation_Results: Crop prices, production costs and yields were most influential; social interaction and lower risk aversion accelerated adoption of unfamiliar practices, and behavioural assumptions materially changed predicted nitrate loads and policy performance.
Evaluation_Scale: 50 hypothetical farmer agents / 50 agricultural subbasins; watershed scale; 1985–2000 simulation period
Limitation_Categories: Real-world validation; Uncertainty; Reproducibility/data availability; Other — semi-hypothetical farmer behaviour
Reported_Limitations: Farmer-behaviour validation is difficult because suitable empirical decision data are limited; the 50-farmer behavioural population is semi-hypothetical and the full decision model is partly documented elsewhere due to space limits.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Collect empirical behavioural data through interviews, role-playing or historical records; improve calibration/validation of farmer decision rules and extend the framework to additional water-quality/bioenergy policy questions.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Hydrologic model/calibration and farmer model Sections 3.1–3.5, pp.4–10; evaluation Section 4, pp.10–14; Conclusions/Future Work, pp.14–15
